title: Why imputation works: haplotypes

blocks.what_we_do:
Reading, about 2 minutes. You can come back to it later.

Learn the idea behind imputation: long shared stretches of chromosome, called haplotypes.
blocks.why:
You inherit one copy of each chromosome from each parent. The sequence of alleles along one copy is called a [haplotype](docs/glossary.md#haplotype).

Chromosomes are passed on in large blocks. Recombination cuts and rejoins them only a few times per chromosome in each generation. So people who are distantly related share long stretches of the same haplotype. Everybody in a population is distantly related to everybody else.

Because of this, alleles at nearby sites are not independent. If you know the alleles at a few sites, you can often predict the alleles at the sites in between. This non-random association between alleles at nearby sites is called linkage disequilibrium ([LD](docs/glossary.md#ld)). You met LD at step 3.4, when we pruned variants that carry the same information.

Imputation uses the same idea in the opposite direction. Pruning removes sites that we can predict from their neighbours. Imputation adds sites that we can predict from their neighbours. It uses a [reference panel](docs/glossary.md#reference-panel): a large group of people whose whole genome was sequenced. If the measured sites of your sample match a stretch in the panel, the panel tells us what lies in the gaps.
blocks.you_need: LD pruning at step 3.4 helps, but it is not required. No data are needed.
blocks.command: No code to run. This is a reading-only step.
blocks.expected_result: You can explain why a few measured sites can predict the sites between them.
blocks.troubleshooting: If the idea is not clear, read the glossary entries for haplotype and LD, then read the step again.
blocks.quick_check:
Why can imputation predict a site that the array did not measure, but not a site where nobody in the reference panel carries the variant?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Imputation copies alleles from matching haplotypes in the reference panel. If no reference haplotype carries the variant, there is nothing to copy. Imputation can only predict variants that exist in the panel.

</details>

student_summary: We see why the alleles at nearby DNA sites can be predicted from each other. People share long stretches of the same chromosome copy, so a few measured sites point to the unmeasured ones in between.
